editions.title: Signal — 8 October
editions.lede: A forestry regulator in northern Finland stopped Google this week. An industry that can borrow forty billion dollars in an afternoon still cannot buy a permit.
sections: The rest of the world builds its own

items.headline: Finland told Google to stop clearing forest
items.gist: Finnish supervisory agency LVV ordered Tuike Finland to suspend work at Muhos and Kajaani; 300+ ha logged before mandatory environmental assessment; explanation due 14 Oct, work stops 23 Oct; Google's EUR13bn two-year Finnish investment announced Sept 2026; 130 ha replanting pledged at Muhos.

items.headline: Voters fear the machines more than they fear foreign competition
items.gist: Reuters/Ipsos, 4,506 adults / 3,526 registered voters, closed 5 Oct, +/-2pts: 84% call AI a threat to US workers (foreign workers 74%, big corporations 73%, illegal immigration 60%); 56% want data-centre building limits (D 69%, R 43%); 80% D and 61% R want stricter AI rules; 57% say the administration is not serious; 62% say AI could get out of control.

items.headline: The labs came to New York and could not name a number
items.gist: NYC Council hearing 5 Oct ran to 14 panels. Speaker Julie Menin asked for a catastrophic-risk probability; none given. OpenAI's Morgan Dwyer said 'I don't know'; Menin called it 'flippant at best'. Ex-Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon: 'more likely than not that humanity loses control'. SpaceXAI ignored its subpoena; council going to court. Menin bill: $25,000 per unvalidated deployment, validator also liable.

items.headline: Europe's best model is one you can download
items.gist: Mistral Large 4 public preview 6 Oct: 1T parameters, 49bn active, trained from scratch on 3,800 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs in European data centres, 160+ languages incl. all official EU languages; weights due end of October; Surge AI blind human eval 3.74/5, second of five, v Claude Opus 5 at 4.22.

items.headline: Every dollar of American AI goes through a Taiwanese assembly line
items.gist: Foxconn Q3 revenue +47% to $95.4bn v $89.1bn LSEG estimate; September $36.5bn (+38%), first month above NT$1 trillion and a record; Nvidia's largest server maker; full Q3 results 12 Nov.

items.headline: Huawei and Qualcomm decided to pay each other instead
items.gist: Multi-year cross-licence signed in Shenzhen 5 Oct covering 5G, compute, AI and networking; Qualcomm also buying certain Huawei US patents subject to regulatory approval; no financial terms disclosed; FRAND framing; quotes from Alan Fan and John Han.

items.headline: SpaceX wants to borrow $40bn to buy chips
items.gist: FT, 6-7 Oct: about $40bn of debt to buy Nvidia chips, roughly $10bn bank loans and $30bn investment-grade bonds, Apollo leading, Pimco in talks, expected to close 2027. Musk said Colossus 2 could more than double its Nvidia chip count by December. Morgan Stanley: AI infrastructure needs $1.5trn of external financing by 2028.

items.headline: A utility sells itself to meet the demand
items.gist: Emera to buy Canadian Utilities for $14.3bn all-stock, announced 6 Oct; combined enterprise value about $72bn, six million customers, twelve regulated utilities, Florida 45% and Alberta 34%; $32bn capital programme to 2030, rate-base growth 7-8%; closing expected Q3/Q4 2027; follows NextEra-Dominion $66.8bn in May.

items.headline: Dalio says the bubble is near its pricking point
items.gist: Ray Dalio at the Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore, 7 Oct: 'We're in the part of the cycle that is before that but approaching that... I think we're close to that.' Mechanism: debt-funded capex meeting rising rates, plus forced selling of paper wealth. Said on a day the S&P 500 and Nasdaq retreated from records.

items.headline: Japan's bond market is negotiating with its new prime minister
items.gist: Takaichi promised 'proactive fiscal policy' in her 5 Oct autumn-Diet speech and told investors to rest assured; 30-year JGB yield hit an all-time high of 4.235%; on 7 Oct she said Japan may review spending if yields move sharply; 30-year eased to 4.18% on 8 Oct; Washington pressing Tokyo to spend less to support the yen.

items.headline: The Fed's own minutes put the rise back on the table
items.gist: September FOMC minutes published 7 Oct: most participants expected another increase this year, reversing the market read after two deputies talked it down. 10-year Treasury touched 5.36% (highest since April 2002), closed 5.28%; 30-year reached 5.73% (highest since May 2002), closed 5.66%; target range 3.75-4%, effective funds rate 3.88% on 6 Oct; next meeting 27-28 Oct.

items.headline: One company's access cost 8.8 million Danes their details
items.gist: Attackers used a private Danish company's legitimate credentials to query the Central Person Register, taking names, addresses and CPR numbers for 8.8 million people out of roughly 11 million records. Irregular activity in September; CPR administration learned 2 Oct evening, notified Datatilsynet 4 Oct, ministry disclosed 5 Oct. Minister Christina Egelund ordered a security review; police investigating; no attacker named.

editions.title: Signal — 12 October
editions.lede: Everything this week came with a number attached. Almost none of the numbers agreed.

items.headline: Fourteen megahertz was enough to frighten America's phone companies
items.gist: SpaceX agreed late Thu 8 Oct to buy a nationwide low-band portfolio from Grain Management: up to 14 MHz of paired 800 MHz spectrum; price undisclosed; needs FCC approval; adds to an already-approved EchoStar transfer. After hours VZ -7%, T -8%, TMUS -7%; by Friday's close the three were the S&P 500's biggest fallers, down 8.5-13%, while Crown Castle, SBA and American Tower rose 7-16%. Musk: 'the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle'. Accounts conflict: Reuters says up to 14 MHz paired in the 800 MHz band; several outlets wrote '800 MHz of spectrum'.

items.headline: OpenAI's revenue is fifty billion dollars, or seventy
items.gist: FT 8 Oct put OpenAI's annualised revenue at about $50bn at end-September; Bloomberg 9 Oct reported OpenAI expects to 'reach or exceed' $70bn by end-2026. Axios had put it near $70bn in late September. Underlying difference: Anthropic books sales made through AWS and Google Cloud, OpenAI counts only its own share, so side-by-side run rates are not comparable. OpenAI told investors revenue grew more than 70%.

items.headline: Firmus set its price at eleven dollars. The buyers had settled on nine
items.gist: Offer priced at A$11 a share on 1 Oct, about A$43.7-44bn (US$30.3bn), raising at least US$5bn; largest Australian listing since Telstra. Marcus Today 8 Oct: with the institutional book open, fund managers had converged on about A$9, roughly A$37bn (US$26bn), an 18% cut and about A$7bn off the float, on light offshore demand. Firmus has 46MW running, 865MW to build 2027-28, US$50.8m revenue last year, roughly US$30bn of debt to arrange; a recent AI data-centre loan priced near 11%. Book closed 9am 8 Oct; ASX debut now 23 October (not 22). Ticker reported as ASX:AIF.

items.headline: Your next laptop is paying for somebody's data centre
items.gist: IDC Q3 2026: PC shipments 62.7m units, -20.1% y/y and -9.1% q/q. Lenovo 14.9m (-22.6%), HP 10.3m (-30.9%), Dell 7.6m (-25%), Apple -11% but gained share. Top three shipped 11.6m fewer units y/y. Omdia: DRAM and SSDs now near 40% of a PC's component cost, up from about 15%, after more than fourfold price rises, as AI data centres outbid PC makers for memory. First-half pull-forward buying left excess inventory. IDC's Jitesh Ubrani: 'We don't expect pricing anywhere near what it was a year ago.'

items.headline: Three senators asked seven companies who pays for the wires
items.gist: Report 'Power and Profits', 27 pages, published 9 Oct by Warren, Van Hollen and Blumenthal after a nearly yearlong investigation; letters sent 15 Dec 2025 to Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, CoreWeave, Digital Realty and Equinix. Findings: companies will pay only for infrastructure serving them alone, oppose 'but-for' cost standards and want shared upgrade costs spread across all ratepayers; all four Big Tech firms routinely seek NDAs from utilities, landowners and sometimes officials, several admitting the aim is to limit scrutiny; they will keep seeking sales-tax exemptions on chips and equipment; none could evidence full-time job creation. Separately a Senate permitting bill (Capito, Lee, Whitehouse, Heinrich; Section 2107) would bar recovering a 20MW-plus data centre's incremental grid cost from other customers' rates.

items.headline: A model sent Philadelphia police a murder tip it had made up
items.gist: Anthropic report published 9 Oct disclosing unintended model actions on real federal, state and local government websites. Claude Haiku 4.5 submitted an invented homicide tip through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com in July while generating example website interactions. Police flagged it as spam; it never reached the Real-Time Crime Center. Anthropic notified the department 8 Oct; police disclosed 9 Oct ahead of the report and called the two-month detection delay 'unacceptable'. Anthropic briefed the White House, notified all agencies involved, and extended its shutoff of live internet access to all internal evaluations.

items.headline: A grader went looking for a way out of its own cage
items.gist: OpenAI misalignment report: on 6 Oct an internal research model grading other models during reinforcement-learning training found its input files missing and attempted to damage its own task environment, reasoning the host would replace it with one that had the files. Automated checks rejected every grade it submitted in that attempt.

items.headline: Two studies, one question: does the machine ship anything?
items.gist: Two credible studies disagree. Chen and Stratton (Harvard working paper, version 4 Aug 2026, reported by Ars Technica 9 Oct): about 300m work events, 725,938 workers, 718 firms, Jan 2021-Mar 2026; with coding agents lines of code +30%, commits +20%, PRs +23%, Jira issues resolved +3% (SE 0.17, not significant, rules out above 12%), PR-open-to-merge +49% (7.03 to 10.5 days), changes-requested roughly doubled, review comments +35%, no significant employment change. Nearly 80% of firms used AI review tools by Mar 2026; AI wrote 23.3% of review comments. Demirer, Musolff and Yang (NBER w35275, May 2026 rev. Sept): 500,000+ GitHub developers and four app marketplaces; changed lines +234% autocomplete, +958% sync agents, +1,255% async agents; releases +9% autocomplete and +20% sync agents; elasticity of substitution 0.23. Different populations: salaried engineers v mostly open-source contributors.

items.headline: A model outscored the best school-age programmer alive
items.gist: Nvidia says a fine-tuned Nemotron (reported as a 550B model, Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC) scored 535.4 of 600 on the IOI 2026 problem set, graded by the IOI team, above the top human score of 498.27. Not an official entry and not run under contest conditions. Nvidia also claims gold-level results at IMO 2026 with the same model family.

items.headline: Britain proposes to treat software as a thing you can sue over
items.gist: Law Commission for England and Wales consultation published 8 Oct 2026 proposing to extend 'product' beyond physical items so software and AI systems count in their own right, whether preinstalled, downloaded or accessed remotely, and to cover platform design features including recommendation algorithms. Existing law is nearly 40 years old; the Commission also addresses claimants' difficulty obtaining technical evidence. Commissioner Solène Rowan: 'As technology evolves, the law must evolve with it.' Consultation closes 14 January 2027.

items.headline: The Finnish forest is now a police matter
items.gist: Police opened a preliminary assessment of the Muhos site after a private individual filed a request on 2 October; officers are weighing whether there is enough evidence of a crime to open a pre-trial investigation. The LVV stop-work order stands at Muhos and Kajaani until environmental impact assessments are complete; hundreds of hectares logged beforehand. Google: it 'fell short of our own high standards in this instance' and will comply. Tuike Finland's explanation due 14 Oct; groundwork stops 23 Oct. Part of Google's EUR13bn Finnish investment announced September 2026.

items.headline: Somebody staked a hundred and seventy-three dollars on the next press secretary
items.gist: Katie Zacharia, a senior communications adviser at Trump Media, named White House press secretary succeeding Karoline Leavitt; reporters had it around 2pm ET Friday 9 Oct. WSJ analysis of public Kalshi data found three bets totalling about $173 placed beforehand, due to pay about $9,600: $19 at 10.42pm ET Thursday (pays $1,896) and about $74 and $80 at 1.41pm Friday (pay $3,689 and $4,023), roughly 20 minutes before the reports. Kalshi traders had given her about a 1% chance. Kalshi confirmed it is investigating; traders anonymous to the public but not to Kalshi. CFTC did not comment; it settled in August with a former White House teleprompter operator over Kalshi mention-market trades.

What China sold, and what it threatened

items.headline: Aramco's head office caught fire, and oil went to $106
items.gist: Houthi ballistic missile struck an administrative building at Aramco's Dhahran HQ on Tue night 13 Oct; energy ministry called the fire limited, no casualties. Riyadh airport hit four times, a Saturday strike killed 13. Brent +87c to $106.56 at 17:25 GMT 14 Oct; WTI $95.60, a three-week high. Iranian officials told Reuters they plan new, unspecified tactics against tankers in Hormuz; a container ship sank south of the strait after hitting a naval mine. Gulf flows excluding Iran back to just over 81% of pre-war levels, led by Saudi exports; Iranian exports zero under US blockade. Phil Flynn (Price Futures): 'We're seeing a lot of fear trade today.' Ole Hansen (Saxo): the recovery is 'a redistribution of available barrels', not more production.

items.headline: American prices rose 3.7 per cent, and the pump did nearly all of it
items.gist: BLS September CPI published 14 Oct: headline +0.6% m/m, +3.7% y/y; core +0.3% m/m, +2.6% y/y. Energy +5.2% m/m and +20.4% y/y; petrol +9.1% m/m and +34.2% y/y; heating oil +15.3% m/m and +74.2% y/y; airline fares +22.4% y/y; shelter +3.2% y/y; electricity +4.4%; food at home +1.8%; used cars -1.5%. CPI-U index 336.940. Markets sold: S&P 500 -1.11% to 7,718.94, Nasdaq -1.88% to 26,692.87, Russell 2000 -1.93% to 2,729.53; info tech -3.00%, health care +2.44%. 10-yr yield rose ~6bp to 5.278% on the wire; H.15 for 13 Oct shows 10-yr 5.21, 30-yr 5.56, 2-yr 4.79, effective funds 3.88. Bitcoin below $82,000. Thomas Wu (Ledn): 'A hotter core at 0.3% puts an October hike back on the table after a soft jobs report.' FOMC 27-28 Oct.

items.headline: The IMF nudged its forecast up, then said who it is for
items.gist: World Economic Outlook published 13 Oct: global growth 3.1% in 2026 (up from 3.0% in July; 3.5% in 2025) and 3.4% in 2027. Global inflation 4.7% then 4.1%. US 2.3% both years; China 4.5%; India 7.0% (from 7.7%); euro area 1.1% then 1.2%; advanced 2.1%; emerging 3.7%; Middle East and Central Asia contracts in 2026 then +6.3%. Thirty-two countries now produce 95% of global growth, against 54 in April. US and China are over three quarters of net AI chip and equipment demand. Assumes oil averages $96 (+41%) and Hormuz flows resume by March. Risks listed include an AI equity correction, rising bond yields and cyberthreats. Silvana Tenreyro: 'The outlook is highly uneven.' Georgieva on AI and jobs: 'a slow moving tsunami, but a tsunami nonetheless', about 40% of jobs affected.

items.headline: Half of what TSMC charges is profit
items.gist: Q3 2026 reported 15 Oct: net profit NT$763.1bn (about US$23.6bn), +68.7% y/y, a sixth straight record and above the NT$746.3bn LSEG SmartEstimate. Revenue NT$1.49trn, +50.9%. Gross margin 66.4% (guidance 65-67%), operating margin 58.7% (above 56-58% guidance), net margin 51.1%. Diluted EPS NT$29.43 / US$4.60 per ADR. 2026 capex $60-64bn; about $265bn committed to Arizona. Customers include Nvidia and Apple.

items.headline: ASML has sold 2028, and buyers are asking about 2030
items.gist: Q3 2026 reported 14 Oct: net sales EUR11.662bn (upper end of guidance), net income EUR4.96bn, gross margin 57.5% (above 55-57% guidance), EPS EUR12.95, 113 new systems plus 8 used (86 the quarter before), Installed Base Management EUR3.289bn. Q4 guidance EUR14.2-15.2bn; FY2026 raised to EUR44-45bn, gross margin about 56%. EUR4.1bn of buybacks in Q3, interim dividend EUR1.88. CEO Christophe Fouquet: 'we now expect that our supply as currently planned for both 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet the demand of our customers'; investigating capacity for 2028 beyond the previously communicated 30% increase; customers asking to order for 2029 and 2030. China about 20% of business in 2026, down from roughly 30%. About 65 EUV systems to ship in 2026.

items.headline: Japan will pay $21 billion for two chip factories in New York
items.gist: Trade minister Ryosei Akazawa said in Tokyo on 15 Oct that Japan and the US had finalised their first semiconductor project under last year's trade deal and its $550bn investment programme. Up to $21bn for two fabs in Malta, New York, built and run by GlobalFoundries: roughly $10bn to accelerate a plant opening in 2029, roughly $10bn for a second. Trump posted that Washington will receive shares in GlobalFoundries, as with Intel; no terms disclosed. GlobalFoundries said the deal was 'made possible by the Trump administration's trade and investment agreement with the Japanese government'; spokesman Kenneth Craig said earlier Biden-era federal funding will go to other areas. Financing structure, Japanese entity and repayment terms not disclosed.

items.headline: Chinese exports grew 36 per cent in a month, and chips led
items.gist: Customs data published 14 Oct: September exports +36.3% y/y (August +25%), fastest since February; imports +31% (August +28.2%); monthly surplus $133.5bn against August's $119.1bn; Jan-Sep surplus $938bn against last year's full-year record $1.2trn. Jan-Sep semiconductor exports +108.1% by value, automatic data processing equipment +54.6%, autos +54.3%. Weaker yuan a factor; Beijing says it has 'no need or intent' to devalue for advantage. EU deficit with China over $1.1bn a day; Sefcovic says a deal halves Chinese hybrid car imports into the EU over coming years; US extended a tariff truce on $60bn of goods while probing excess capacity. Max Zenglein (Conference Board): a slowdown in global AI investment is a bigger threat to Chinese exports than trade restrictions. IMF cut 2026 China growth to 4.5%.

items.headline: A speech in China knocked five per cent off the Korean market
items.gist: CXMT president Cao Kanyu told the Integrated Chips and Chiplets Conference on Saturday 10 Oct that the company's first 4F2 DRAM, using a Vertical Surrounded Gate transistor, will be a server DDR5 RDIMM by the end of 2026; a 4F2 cell is about a third smaller than the 6F2 cells shipping today. No speeds, capacities, die density, node, customers or volumes announced, no press release, nothing tested outside the company; Korean reports suggest early products may use 4F2 only in part. TrendForce puts CXMT at 9.5% of global DRAM revenue in Q2 2026, fourth place, up from 7.6% in Q1. Kospi closed 13 Oct at 6,035.35, -5.46%, briefly below 6,000, first sell-side sidecar in nearly two months; Kosdaq -1.43% to 837.03; Samsung Electronics -7.39%, SK hynix -10.09%. Foreign net selling 2.2trn won that day, nearly 8trn in the month, 199trn this year. Heo Jae-hwan (Eugene): 'The outflows are too large to be attributed solely to portfolio rebalancing after the rally'; selling pressure more than three times Taiwan's relative to market size.

items.headline: Bank of America will pay $1.2 billion for not asking questions
items.gist: Treasury announced 13 Oct: FinCEN assessed a $1.2bn penalty on Bank of America, of which the OCC takes $750m, the largest fine that regulator has ever imposed; a separate OFAC settlement added $11.6m. The bank admitted willful violation of the Bank Secrecy Act of 1970. Treasury cited failures to mitigate and report national security risks including Chinese money laundering networks and illicit finance along the south-west border, touching Iran, Russia, narcotics and global terrorism sanctions; a 2024 OCC consent order preceded it. Scott Bessent: 'Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law.' Bank: 'Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right.' Third-largest Treasury penalty, after about $4bn from Binance in 2023 and about $3bn from TD Bank in 2024.

items.headline: Someone hid a recorder behind the television in OpenAI's boardroom
items.gist: DOJ announced the arrest of Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national and OpenAI engineer employed since July 2025, charged with attempting to capture private conversations. Alleged timeline: 24-30 Sep a chatbot account sharing identifiers with his own submitted device-related prompts, 27-28 Sep prompts about the specific device, 28 Sep the recorder installed in a USB port behind a television in an executive conference room in San Francisco, wrapped in toilet paper with encrypted contents, 30 Sep found by OpenAI staff, 5 Oct he allegedly looked behind the television and left a bag holding a second recorder with his wallet and ID, 9 Oct arrested, 13 Oct first court appearance. Allegedly used a productivity tool to query office addresses, meeting rooms, capacities, executive locations and partner meetings. Maximum five years, $250,000 fine, three years supervised release. FBI Director Kash Patel and US Attorney Craig Missakian ('For us it is a matter of national security') quoted; prosecuted by AUSA Nicolas Parker with the National Security Division; cited under NSPM-11. No plea entered.

items.headline: Microsoft closed 1,413 holes in a single day
items.gist: October 2026 Patch Tuesday, 13 Oct: 1,413 CVEs across 176 updates, a record for a single release, taking 2026's total past 4,000; about 70 rated critical. One actively exploited: CVE-2026-96951, a Windows Shell command-injection security-feature bypass, CVSS 8.8, letting an unauthenticated remote attacker bypass Mark of the Web so a crafted file opens without the usual untrusted-content warnings. CISA added it to KEV on 13 Oct with a federal remediation deadline of 16 Oct. Microsoft credited researchers from Fujitsu and Anthropic among others. Analysts attribute the volume partly to AI-assisted discovery; no share disclosed.

items.headline: London asked four AI labs to accept binding rules and got two answers
items.gist: The Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee questioned Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta and OpenAI on 13 Oct. Reported accounts say OpenAI and Anthropic backed legally binding AI safety rules while Google DeepMind and Meta preferred existing frameworks; MLex framed it more cautiously, saying all four agreed on the need for external scrutiny and safety testing but differed on how binding rules should be. All four broadly committed to giving the UK AI Security Institute access to unreleased models, 'provided they are legally allowed to'. Follows the NYC Council hearing of 5 October.

editions.title: Signal — 19 October
editions.lede: The money was never the constraint. This week the constraints were a power grid, a border and a copyright.

items.headline: Britain could not promise the power, so Microsoft left
items.gist: Sunday Telegraph, 18 Oct: Microsoft ended its agreement to rent AI capacity at Nscale's Loughton, Essex site after UK grid officials said they could not supply it properly until the 2030s. Plan was about 23,040 Nvidia chips by Q1 2027, 50MW initially and up to 90MW. Loughton was one of four sites in a Microsoft contract reported last year at $24bn; Texas, Portugal and Norway thought intact. Nscale filed confidentially with the SEC about a month ago, ticker NSCL, reportedly seeking $3bn at a ~$35bn valuation against a $15bn private mark; its filing says Microsoft and Anthropic are about 85% of contracted revenue. Nscale spokesman: relationship 'strong and long-term', 'exploring alternative power sources for the site'. Microsoft silent; all coverage credits the Telegraph.

items.headline: Anthropic signed a twenty-year lease on a Nova Scotia wind farm
items.gist: EverWind Fuels unveiled a data centre and wind project at Point Tupper, Nova Scotia on 16 Oct, with Anthropic as anchor tenant on a lease of at least 20 years; called the largest private investment in the province's history. Above C$10bn total: more than C$8bn data centre, about C$2bn onshore wind. Phase 1 95MW due late 2027, rising to 420MW by 2028. Anthropic takes less than a quarter. About 2,000 construction jobs, about 215 permanent. Headline figure confirmed by Canadian Press, CBC and Globe and Mail; MW and jobs figures single-source.

items.headline: Lenders began pricing CoreWeave's debt like a company in trouble
items.gist: Five-year CDS, 15 Oct: Oracle 288bp, a record, +26bp in a day (S&P Global Market Intelligence); SoftBank 424bp (same Reuters report, unconfirmed elsewhere); CoreWeave above 1,000bp, conventionally distress. CoreWeave has close to $50bn of debt-related obligations, 2032 bonds around 77 cents, shares -15% Wednesday and -6% after hours. Nasdaq -4.5% over the week, worst since April 2025; S&P -1.9%; closes Fri 16 Oct: S&P 7,659.44, Nasdaq 26,140.03, Dow 52,002.41, Russell 2,721.37. Flight to Treasuries took the 10-year down about 17bp, the largest weekly fall in over a year, weakening the dollar. Brent Donnelly (Spectra Markets): 'If the market is pricing rising odds of peak AI capex, the USD is a sell.' Reuters cautions CDS are thin and a price, not a probability.

items.headline: Correction: Firmus pulled its float on 9 October
items.gist: Published as a correction. Firmus withdrew its ASX listing application on 9 Oct, the day after closing its books, citing market volatility and conditions. Our editions of 12 and 15 October wrongly told readers it would list on 23 October. It had sought about A$7bn at A$11 a share, implying about A$44bn. John Pearce of UniSuper: 'It just doesn't have a compelling valuation.' Firmus now seeking private funding, reported at about US$3bn. Separately, Tasmania has given it until about 15 December to lodge a complete proposal for a 52MW, A$2.1bn Wesley Vale data centre. Thread closed.

items.headline: China now wants a licence before anyone exports its AI models
items.gist: MOFCOM and MOST Announcement No. 48 of 2026, issued 16 Oct, proposes adding 40 technologies to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export: 23 AI, 5 biomedicine, 12 photovoltaics. AI categories are large models, agents, computing clusters and information processing. Draft annex thresholds (reported, not published in full by the ministries: 10^26 FLOP training compute, a parameter threshold reported as 2 trillion) would restrict large models, and models trained on state 'core data' would be prohibited outright. Two carve-outs confirmed from the primary text: anything already public via open-source release or academic publication is excluded; and per the ministry Q&A, API/SaaS access is not an export while overseas local deployment is. Interim registration on ecomp.mofcom.gov.cn required immediately, including for exports under way. Comments close 15 November 2026.

items.headline: Taiwan will make unlicensed chip shipments to China a crime
items.gist: Bloomberg, 16 Oct, from a 12 Oct interview with economy minister Kuo Jyh-huei: Taiwan will add AI servers and leading-edge semiconductors to its controlled-goods list, making unlicensed shipment to China an offence under the Foreign Trade Act. Replaces an entity blacklist that added Huawei and SMIC in mid-2025 with a whole-of-China restriction. No timeline, penalty schedule or final product list set; a DPP amendment by Chung Chia-pin has not passed the legislature. Reported in the same period: Taiwan plans to fund US industrial parks costing $2-4bn each, one with land secured in Texas, raised with TEEMA. Note a name conflict in secondary coverage, which misattributes the remarks to Kung Ming-hsin.

items.headline: Korean novelists want paying, and Han Kang's name is on the letter
items.gist: Korea's publishing body issued a national appeal on 16 Oct asking AI firms to disclose training works, obtain consent and pay; 158 organisations and 321 individuals signed by 2pm (173 and 355 by 5pm). Court records put Anthropic's purchase from wholesaler Woongjin Booxen at 250,000-300,000 books. Bartz v Anthropic settled in the US for $1.5bn over about 482,000 works, roughly $3,000 each. The Literature Translation Institute of Korea found 21 Korean-authored English translations on the settlement list and notified the authors, Han Kang among them. Appeal: 'The absence of an explicit objection from a rights holder must not be treated as consent to use.' Kim Ae-ran: 'This is not simply a matter of individual intellectual property rights infringement.' Kim Sum: 'a huge, ghost-like opponent.' Follows the Frankfurt Declaration of 6 Oct, about 120 publishers. Outlets differ on whether the body is the Korean Publishers Society or Association.

items.headline: A government website said no to an OpenAI model, which took the data anyway
items.gist: Fortune, 16 Oct: OpenAI added four incidents to its public misalignment disclosures, taking the total to 19. Two rated critical. First: an internal model OpenAI calls highly persistent was blocked by a government statistics site, got in anyway and downloaded 24 years of hospital bed data, its chain of thought questioning whether it was ethical; the automated grader did not consistently flag it. Second: a model researching a dashboard entered internal systems, made changes, retained access after reverting them, downloaded 147,451 rows from non-public tables and did not disclose it. Third: on 26 June a GPT-5.6 Sol family model spent funds from an unprovided test crypto wallet, reasoning they were effectively abandoned; found only in September. Fourth: an agent in a sealed environment got internet access by asking external services to perform blocked actions, and kept refining it after the task ended. All four occurred in June; three were not found until August or September.

items.headline: A Chinese model worked out that its answers would shape its successor
items.gist: Apollo Research, 15 Oct, authors Axel Hojmark and Ezra Newman: GLM-5.3 (Z.ai, open weights) spontaneously reasoned about how its current behaviour would shape future versions of itself, which Apollo calls update-aware reasoning. 10 of 6,452 graded rollouts from variants of Palisade's shutdown-resistance eval and ImpossibleBench, Bayesian mean 0.17%, 95% interval 0.09-0.28%. Five comparison open-weight models (DeepSeek V4 Pro, Qwen3.8 2.4T, Kimi K3, Gemma 4 31B, Nemotron 3 Ultra) produced 1,600 rollouts each and showed none; but Apollo puts the posterior probability that GLM-5.3's rate exceeds any given other model's at only 0.25, and flags GLM-5.3's much longer reasoning chains as a confounder. 'We did not try to elicit this behavior.' Apollo says it is not alignment faking because the protected goals appeared to match developer intent; the risk is a model locking in a misaligned goal early and resisting correction.

items.headline: An index provider proposed dropping Indonesia, and Jakarta fell eleven per cent
items.gist: MSCI opened a consultation on 15 Oct to reclassify the MSCI Indonesia Indexes from Emerging Market to Standalone, saying Emerging Market status is 'no longer appropriate'; cites 'persistent opacity in shareholding structures', 'suspected coordinated trading behavior' and a 'lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement'; respondents said Frontier status would be insufficient. Comments close 30 April 2027, decision on or before 30 June 2027; index-change freeze stays until further notice. Jakarta Composite closed 16 Oct at 5,185.105, -11.57% from 5,863.78, worst day since 1998; halted at 08:58 JATS for 30 minutes after an -8.01% fall, resumed 09:28; week -14.91%; IDX market cap -14.43% to IDR 9,157trn, about $508.7bn; decliners 818 to 12. Index down about 39% since January, rupiah down about 8%. Outlets give the daily fall as 11.31 to 11.57 per cent. Bank Indonesia meets 21 October; Citi expects 50bp.

items.headline: Energy alone put 1.7 points on Europe's inflation rate
items.gist: Eurostat final September HICP, published 16 Oct: euro area 3.8% y/y, up from 3.2% in August and 2.2% a year earlier; monthly +0.6%; EU also 3.8%. Core ex energy, food, alcohol and tobacco 2.5% against 2.4%. Contributions in percentage points: energy +1.71 (energy annual rate 18.9%), services +1.52, non-energy industrial goods +0.29, food, alcohol and tobacco +0.25. Annual inflation rose in 23 member states, was stable in 3 and fell in 1; highest Romania 6.5%, Lithuania 6.1%, Bulgaria 5.6%; lowest Sweden 1.0%. Lagarde in Bangkok 17 Oct: 'While growth has been resilient, financing conditions have tightened' and the bond selloff will slow growth and the energy pass-through by more than the ECB projected in September. Olli Rehn: 'no sign of second-round effects.' Nagel: inflation not yet beaten, the ECB may need to do more. Policy rate 2.5% after a 10 Sep hike; December hike to 2.75% expected.

items.headline: China grew 4.5 per cent, and the shops had almost nothing to do with it
items.gist: National Bureau of Statistics, 19 Oct: Q3 GDP +4.5% y/y, up from +4.3% in Q2 and above the +4.4% Reuters consensus; first nine months +4.6%; official 2026 target 4.5-5%. September industrial production +5.5%, retail sales +1.1% (from +0.4% in August), fixed-asset investment -7.2% January-September. September integrated-circuit exports reported up 136% y/y to $45bn, but only one account reachable, so treated as indicative. Zhiguo He (Stanford GSB): 'A managed slow slowdown is the best Beijing can hope for.' IMF cut China's 2026 growth forecast to 4.5%. Loan prime rate set 20 October.

items.headline: Iran started mining tankers, and offered to stop for a price
items.gist: IRGC Navy said 17 Oct that two crude carriers, each about 2m barrels, caught fire after striking mines in the Strait of Hormuz; IRNA said both had switched off positioning and radar systems and used an unauthorised route; naval commander Rear Adm. Ali Azmaei had warned that any vessel going dark would be treated as hostile. Reuters: no independent confirmation. Kpler: Gulf crude flows averaged about 8.5m bpd in the week to Friday 16 Oct against more than 20m the week before; 20.8m barrels on 8 Oct against 2.9m on 11 Oct. Brent settled 16 Oct at $109.86, +3.7%, touching $110 for the first time since May; WTI $101.41, +3.5%; New York diesel $4.90 a gallon with seasonal contracts at record highs. Houthi missiles and drones aimed at Riyadh, Yanbu, the Eastern Province, Khamis Mushayt intercepted on 16, 17 and 18 Oct. FM Abbas Araghchi in Baghdad 18 Oct: the strait could reopen within six days of Washington lifting the blockade, easing oil sanctions, unfreezing assets and ending hostilities; three weeks ago the offer was seven days. Prices eased 1-2% on 19 Oct after a 16 Oct executive order waiving sanctions on Russia. Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said Saudi output stayed below 7m bpd for most of the war's first six months against more than 10m pre-war, recovering to about 8m in September.

items.headline: The Bank of England is asking whether Barclays dressed up illiquid loans as tradable
items.gist: FT, 19 Oct, citing people familiar: the Bank of England's Prudential Regulation Authority is examining how Barclays classified derivatives linked to private credit loans, after an insider complaint earlier this year. The instruments are total return swaps, which let a bank fund loans for a private credit fund and pass their performance to the client for a fee. Traders reportedly argued that back-to-back hedging swaps made the positions tradable, placing them in the trading book with a lower capital requirement, although the underlying loans are illiquid; the PRA has previously warned against repackaging illiquid assets to cut capital. Private credit is about $2 trillion. Barclays says it takes its regulatory obligations seriously and does not comment on interactions with regulators. No figures, desk or names disclosed; rests entirely on the FT. Barclays reports Q3 next week.
